title: Favourites coming back from behind
question: When the favourite is losing at half-time, does backing it at the in-play price make money?
rule: $1 on the favourite trailing at half-time, at DraftKings' in-play price from the snapshot at kickoff + 55 min.
verdict_text: No. On 732 bets the in-play price paid out less than the stakes: ROI -25.1% (-38.3% to -10.2%). The market already rates these comebacks higher than they happen.

C.label: Design C: eight leagues, 2022/23 to 2024/25 (without B's matches)

phase1.note: Free data, 2017/18 to 2024/25. Favourites who fall behind won more often than a simple model that ignores the score and spreads goals evenly over 90 minutes. About a third of the half-time gap is just that second halves have more goals. This compared against a model, not against any price.

timelines.note: Free ESPN goal timelines, eight leagues, 2017/18 to 2024/25. When the underdog scores first, the favourite beats the score-blind model by a similar 3 to 6 points whatever the minute, so no minute stands out. Testing it at real prices would need about 1,882 snapshots (18,820 credits); not bought.

notes: The price is DraftKings' in-play moneyline on the favourite, taken from the odds archive's snapshot about 55 minutes after kickoff, inside the half-time break. Only quotes updated after kickoff and at most 5 minutes old count.

Phase 1 found favourites come back more often than a simple model says. The market already knows: at half-time it priced the comeback at 21.3% while 17.0% happened (design C), so backing the trailing favourite lost about a quarter of the stake.
Design B's positive season (+7.3%) was not a pattern. C, on prices never seen before, lost 25.1%, and every by-league, by-season and by-band line here is descriptive.

A new idea from these numbers, laying the trailing favourite included, needs its own pre-registration on seasons not used here (2025/26 or later) and the owner's approval before any credits are spent.
